# Decision history — pdf-integrity

Every revision of every decision, plus the terminal revisions of other normative records. Includes archived records: this is the project's memory of what it used to think.

## audit.decision.crate-shape

### Revision 1 — Facts in pdf-read, interpretation in a new pdf-forensics crate

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.crate-shape/1` · scope `all` · topic `crate-shape`

pdf-read remains the neutral facts layer (open health, recovery, xrefs, metadata, annotations, signatures, pages, object roles, representation metrics). One new crate, pdf-forensics, holds logical-revision reconstruction, object-change classification, semantic and visual comparison, evidence generation, and findings policy. pdf-cli gains a development `audit` command; a standalone `lege-pdf-audit` binary ships later over pdf-forensics. The findings engine never lives in pdf-structure, pdf-content, or the renderer, and the initial crate takes no OCR or lege-gpu dependencies.

**Context.** The existing renderer crates report what the PDF says. Mixing suspicion heuristics into them would contaminate a parser that must stay policy-free, and would drag renderer dependencies into a forensic tool that needs a small, auditable footprint.

**Consequences.** Some structural data (per-section xref entries, annotation object identity, operator provenance) must be surfaced by the lege-pdf crates as neutral facts before pdf-forensics can consume them — that is the lege-pdf upgrade work tracked in the lege namespace.

## audit.decision.encrypted-input-handling

### Revision 1 — Encrypted PDFs get a structure-only audit, upgraded by an optional password

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.encrypted-input-handling/1` · scope `all` · topic `encryption`

Encryption is always reported as a neutral fact (version, revision, method, whether the empty user password validates). The checker never refuses an encrypted input. Without a usable password it performs a structure-only audit — file identity, xref-section inventory, object roles and locations, annotation and signature dictionaries, ByteRange, and the feature flags readable without decrypting stream contents — and every part of the report that could not be computed is marked explicitly unavailable rather than absent or zero. Given `--password` (or a validating empty user password), the document is decrypted through pdf-security and the full audit runs, including page representation classification and font and image inventories. The report carries the analysis mode it ran in, so a structure-only audit is never mistaken for a complete one.

**Context.** Encryption was the top gap in the renderer's 11k-PDF corpus sweep, and encrypted documents are common in the workflows this tool serves, so reporting encryption and stopping would make the tool useless exactly where it is needed. pdf-read already computes whether the empty user password genuinely validates against /U, independent of how the document opened, so the upgrade path costs little.

**Consequences.** The AuditReport schema needs an analysis-mode discriminant and an explicit unavailable state for per-section results, which shapes the schema from the first commit rather than being retrofitted. Findings policy must never raise a suspicion finding on the absence of a fact that a structure-only audit could not have reached. Per-revision encryption changes in M2 and M3 diffing still need their own story; that is left to those milestones.

## audit.decision.forensics-repo-home

### Revision 1 — pdf-forensics lives in the pdf-integrity repo, path-depending on lege-pdf

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.forensics-repo-home/1` · scope `all` · topic `repo-home`

The pdf-forensics crate and the audit CLI live in this pdf-integrity repository, as their own Cargo workspace, consuming the lege-pdf renderer crates through path dependencies into /mnt/Samsung980_1TB/Rust-projects/Lege-ecosystem/lege-pdf/render/crates/. The audit binary is `lege-pdf-audit` from the start; no `audit` subcommand is added to the ecosystem's pdf-cli. Facts that pdf-forensics needs but pdf-read does not yet surface remain lege-namespace upgrade work, landed in the Lege-ecosystem repo and consumed here once released.

**Context.** The alternative was joining the Lege-ecosystem workspace next to the renderer crates. In-workspace would have given atomic cross-crate refactors, which matters because several M1 and M2 items extend pdf-read's DocumentReport and pdf-structure's xref types. Out-of-workspace was chosen to keep the forensic tool's dependency surface small and independently auditable, and its release cadence decoupled from the renderer's.

**Consequences.** Every lege-side fact-surfacing change is a two-repo edit: land it in Lege-ecosystem first, then consume it here. Cargo resolves path dependencies into another workspace normally — the depended-on crates keep inheriting from their own workspace root — but the ecosystem root's [patch] entries for jbig2enc-rust and jp2lam do not apply here, so any transitive git-sourced codec dependency must be re-patched in this workspace's root manifest. The M1 acceptance command for pdfverse-identified changes from a pdf-cli invocation to `lege-pdf-audit`.

## audit.decision.product-framing

### Revision 1 — Triage tool, not a fraud detector

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.product-framing/1` · scope `all` · topic `product-framing`

The product is a local PDF integrity and forensic-triage utility that reports recoverable revision history, structural modifications, overlays, rasterization, signature coverage, and document inconsistencies. It detects and explains recoverable tampering indicators; it never claims to determine fraud, and its dispositions are limited to NO_REVIEW_INDICATOR_FOUND, REVIEW_RECOMMENDED, INTEGRITY_FAILURE, and INCONCLUSIVE.

**Context.** Fraud involves intent and external facts. A PDF can reveal that content changed, how, and sometimes exactly what the previous content was; it usually cannot establish why. A flattened raster export (PDF-Verse style) is compatible with both tampering and legitimate scanning. Practitioners draw the same line: incremental saves preserve useful history, but form filling, optimization, signatures and notary stamps also legitimately alter PDFs.

**Consequences.** Some genuinely forged documents (coherent full rewrites, print-edit-rescan) will report INCONCLUSIVE. That is accepted: the alternative is a score the tool cannot defend.

## audit.decision.revision-model

### Revision 1 — Xref sections and logical revisions are separate types

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.revision-model/1` · scope `all` · topic `revision-model`

The structure layer models XrefSection (offset, kind classic/stream, preserved entries, trailer, /Prev, auxiliary_of for /XRefStm, recovery events) separately from LogicalRevision (chronological index, primary section, auxiliary sections, byte range, boundary confidence). Per-revision object changes are classified as Added, Redefined, Freed, or RepeatedIdentically, and affected objects are classified by role (page, contents, font, image XObject, annotation, signature, metadata, and so on). Revision boundaries pair a syntactically valid startxref with its following %%EOF — never a raw %%EOF byte search, which can hit stream data.

**Context.** Today pdf-structure's Revision is only an xref offset plus trailer; the loader merges section entries first-write-wins and discards which objects each section introduced. Hybrid-reference saves currently count as two revisions and linearization stubs count as one, so revisions.len() cannot be read as an edit count.

**Consequences.** This is the single largest lege-pdf refactor the checker requires, and everything in M2 and M3 rests on it. Memory cost of preserved per-section entries is accepted; entries are Arc slices and only materialized when the audit path asks.

## audit.decision.signature-layering

### Revision 1 — Structural signature coverage first, cryptography second, PKI via a mature crate

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.signature-layering/1` · scope `all` · topic `signature-verification`

Signature support lands in two layers. Layer one is purely structural: find /FT /Sig fields, parse signature dictionaries, validate /ByteRange shape and bounds, associate each signature with a logical revision, identify post-signature revisions, and parse DocMDP/FieldMDP policies — reporting structural status without claiming cryptographic validity. Layer two adds CMS/CAdES digest verification, certificate chains, trust, and timestamps, using a mature external cryptographic implementation rather than a homegrown PKI validator. Report digest validity, certificate trust, time validity, later-revision presence, and later-change permission as five separate statuses, never one verdict.

**Context.** This is a deliberate exception to the ecosystem's native-first, in-house-implementation preference: PKI validation is exactly the domain where a homegrown implementation is a liability rather than an asset, alongside the existing Skrifa and JPX exceptions.

**Consequences.** Layer one alone already answers the highest-value question (did anything change after signing, and was it permitted); shipping it first means M4 crypto can slip without blocking the useful product.

## audit.decision.strict-and-tolerant-parse

### Revision 1 — Dual parse assessment instead of a second strict parser

`proposed` · `@audit.decision.strict-and-tolerant-parse/1` · scope `all` · topic `parse-policy`

The checker does not get a separate strict parser initially. It hashes and inventories raw bytes, records every structural anomaly before interpretation, opens through the existing tolerant path, and marks any evidence derived from recovered structure. A RecoveryPolicy enum (AllowAndRecord / Forbid) is added later once the recovery-event surface is proven sufficient.

**Context.** The renderer's tolerant loader is mature and already emits RecoveryEvent for repairs. Writing a parallel strict parser doubles the parsing surface for a v1 that mostly needs honesty about repairs, not refusal to open.

**Consequences.** Until RecoveryPolicy::Forbid exists, signature verification must independently re-check the byte ranges it hashes rather than trusting tolerant-parse offsets.
